title: The Richest Man in Babylon
author: George S. Clason
publication_date: 1926 (as a book, based on earlier pamphlets from 1920s)
target_audience: Readers interested in classic self-improvement literature
Young adults and beginners looking to develop good money habits
Anyone interested in wealth-building and personal prosperity
core_themes: The importance of saving a portion of income
The value of financial discipline and persistence
primary_purpose: To impart timeless financial wisdom through simple stories and parables set in ancient Babylon, teaching readers how to achieve and maintain personal wealth by following basic principles of money management.

structure_format.narrative_style: Didactic parable style, using engaging fictional stories to teach lessons
structure_format.organization: Collection of interrelated stories and parables featuring Babylonian characters
features: Memorable aphorisms and rules of thumb

key_concepts_lessons: Start thy purse to fattening: Save at least 10% of all you earn.
Control thy expenditures: Budget your expenses to ensure savings.
Make thy gold multiply: Invest saved money wisely so it generates additional income.
Guard thy treasures from loss: Avoid investments that sound too good to be true.
Make of thy dwelling a profitable investment: Own your home to reduce living costs.
Insure a future income: Prepare for future needs and retirement.
Increase thy ability to earn: Continuously improve your skills and knowledge.
notable_features: Uses ancient Babylon as a backdrop for financial parables
Simple, memorable rules for money management
Stories and characters make advice easy to recall
Frequently cited in both modern and historical personal finance literature
cultural_historical_context: Written during the 1920s, an era of economic fluctuation, the book's universal principles address the need for financial literacy and stability. Its parable format was novel for personal finance at the time and has helped the lessons endure for generations.
reception_impact: Recognized as a foundational text in personal finance literature
Praised for clarity, simplicity, and practical relevance across decades
Frequently recommended by financial advisors and educators
Some readers find the archaic language challenging, but the stories remain effective and memorable
comparable_titles: Think and Grow Rich by Napoleon Hill
The Millionaire Next Door by Thomas J. Stanley and William D. Danko
Your Money or Your Life by Vicki Robin and Joe Dominguez
The Wealthy Barber by David Chilton
